specification: Perceivo HMAC request signing, signature version v1, as specified in the perceivo_client.signing package docstring in the perceivo-client repository. The canonical request has eleven fields; field 9 is the Perceivo-Organization header verbatim, or the empty string when the header is absent.
secret_note: This key is published deliberately and protects nothing. Each row maps (audience, key_id, method, path, query, body, content_type, organization, timestamp, nonce, secret) to a signature, so the key must be included for any implementation to reproduce a row. It is a fixed test constant. Never configure it as a signing key in any environment: anyone can sign with it. Static analysis tools may report it as a stored secret; it is a public test value.

secret_transport.note: How an issued secret becomes the HMAC key. The key is 32 random bytes. The platform issues it once, at enrolment, as 64 lowercase hex characters, so the caller holds text and the server holds bytes: an implementation must decode the issued text from hex, never encode it. Encoding it as UTF-8 produces a 64-byte key that does not match the server's, and every request fails with a 401. secret_utf8 is not in the issued form, so the positive vectors do not exercise this decoding; secret_transport_vectors does, and includes the signature the incorrect encoding produces.
secret_transport.disclosure_secret_note: A second published test constant, distinct from secret_utf8, that protects nothing. It is in the issued form so the table can exercise hex decoding. Never configure it anywhere.
secret_transport.rule: A str of exactly 64 characters drawn from [0-9a-fA-F] is an issued secret and is hex-decoded; any other str is keyed on its own UTF-8 bytes; a bytes value is the key verbatim. Hex decoding is case-insensitive. Surrounding whitespace is stripped before the form is tested, because a secret read from a file or a shell often carries a trailing newline.
secret_transport.residual: A 64-character passphrase made only of hex characters cannot be told apart from an issued secret and is decoded, because the platform issues secrets only in that form. To key on such text, pass bytes.

notes: Eleven fields, ten '\n' separators, no trailing newline. Field 1 is the constant 'perceivo-hmac-v1' and is never configurable; field 2 is the audience; field 3 is the key id; field 8 is Content-Type; field 9 is the organization; field 11, the nonce, is last.

Fields 1-3 and 9 must be bound, not merely present. A signed field that the verifier never compares with a value it holds itself provides no protection, because the signer chooses its value. Field 1 is compared for exact equality; field 2 with the verifier's configured audience; field 3 with the id of the key whose secret was used. Field 8 is not bound: it is signed so it cannot be altered in transit, and the server reads the header itself when it parses the body.

Field 9 must be bound even though field 8 is not. The organization selects the tenant the request is authorised against, so the verifier must confirm that the signed value equals the Perceivo-Organization header it received. Make that comparison after compare_digest has accepted the signature: before then, both values are unauthenticated client input. Vector n07 distinguishes an implementation that binds field 9 from one that only signs it.

The negative_vectors list contains correctly signed canonical requests that must be rejected. A bare MAC check accepts every one of them. Reject them all with the same outcome: a distinct reason per check tells an attacker which check failed.

The negative vectors fall into three classes, given by 'refused_by': 'arity' rows (n01, n02, n06) are rejected on the field count before any other check; 'prelude_binding' rows (n03, n04, n05) carry all eleven fields and are rejected on the content of fields 1-3; the 'metadata_binding' row (n07) has correct fields 1-3 and is rejected only after the MAC check, on field 9. Check 'field_count' for each row as well as the rejection: a prelude_binding row with the wrong field count would be rejected on arity and leave the field 1-3 checks untested.

The audience is a deployment label, assigned by the server and configured on both sides. It is not a hostname or the Host header, and is never derived from the request: a verifier that read it from the request would compare the client's value with itself.

key_id is the API key id as a lowercase hyphenated 8-4-4-4-12 UUID, not the key prefix, which every key in an organization shares. v28 supplies the same UUID in uppercase and must produce v01's signature. Normalise by parsing the UUID and rendering it again, so the only outcomes are the correct signature or a rejection.

content_type is the Content-Type request header verbatim: not normalised, not case-folded, parameters not removed. An absent header is the empty string (v01, v29), as for the query field. v30 and v31 have identical bodies whose declared multipart boundaries differ, and therefore different signatures; signing only the media type would give them one signature and allow the body to be re-framed. v02, v32 and v33 are three signatures over the same body bytes.

Sign after the body and headers are final. HTTP client libraries generate the multipart boundary themselves, so a signature computed before the client sets Content-Type covers a value the request never carries, and the request fails with a 401.

No field may contain '\n'. A request that would place a newline in a field is unsignable and must be rejected, not escaped. A Content-Type header that appears more than once is also rejected rather than joined or resolved to one value.

Field 8 admits printable ASCII, 0x20-0x7E, only. A Content-Type containing any other byte is unsignable and must be rejected when signing, never escaped or transliterated. This is narrower than RFC 7231, which admits obs-text in a quoted-string. On printable ASCII, latin-1 and UTF-8 decoding agree, so a signer and a verifier that decode header bytes differently still produce the same field. The empty value is allowed (v01, v29).

The unsignable_vectors list is a third kind of vector, distinct from negative_vectors. A negative vector is a correctly signed string a verifier must reject (mac_is_correct is true for all of them). An unsignable vector has no canonical_request and no signature, because the only conforming response to its input is to refuse to sign. Check these by canonicalising the input and requiring an error.
body_base64 null means no body; an empty string means a zero-byte body. Both produce the same digest (see v01 and v18).

The HMAC key is the secret's raw bytes, never a hex or base64 re-encoding of them. For secret_utf8 those bytes are its UTF-8 encoding, which is why every positive vector keys on secret_utf8 directly. An issued secret is different: it is written as hex and must be decoded, as secret_transport describes.

The canonical request is UTF-8 encoded before HMAC. Every positive vector here is ASCII, because raw_path and the query string are percent-encoded on the wire and field 8 is restricted to printable ASCII. The unsignable vectors include the non-ASCII Content-Type values a signer must reject.
The signature covers no authority: neither the Host header nor an absolute-form request target. The audience identifies the deployment instead, and is configured rather than taken from the request.

canonical_path is field 5 and is the normalised path, not raw_path verbatim. Two operations, in this order: (1) percent-decode unreserved characters only (A-Z a-z 0-9 - . _ ~), in either hex case; (2) remove dot segments per RFC 3986 5.2.4. Nothing else changes: '//' is not merged, a trailing '/' is kept, a reserved escape such as '%2F' is not decoded, and an escape step 1 did not decode is not case-normalised. The server applies this transform to every path before routing, and nothing to the query, so the signature covers the path the server acts on. A signer that emits raw_path verbatim fails v22, v23, v25, v26 and v27; one that reverses the two steps fails v27 alone.

The path transform is not injective. v22, v23 and v24 are three request targets with one signature, and so are v25, v26 and v27. A signature therefore covers a set of equivalent targets. This is safe because every target in a set reaches the server as the same normalised path.

canonical_query is field 6 and is the query string verbatim: every byte after the first '?', in the order sent. Nothing is split, sorted, decoded, re-encoded, deduplicated or reassembled. An implementation that sorts fails v03, v04, v06, v15, v20 and v21, and collapses two distinct pairs to a single signature: v19/v20 and v04/v21.

v35 and v36 are the organization pair: the same request differing only in the Perceivo-Organization value, with different signatures. Exactly three positive rows sign a non-empty organization: v34, v35 and v36; the other 33 sign the empty string. An implementation that omitted field 9 would still pass those 33 and fail only v34, v35 and v36. Compare either with v01, the same request with no header: three requests, three signatures.
The five unsignable rows u01-u05 carry 'field_number': 8 and cover the field 8 character set.

u06-u11 are the field 9 unsignable rows ('field_number': 9). Field 9 is rejected, never normalised: uppercase, braced and unhyphenated UUIDs are refused rather than converted to the canonical spelling. This differs from key_id (see v28), which is normalised: key_id is a UUID the server has already resolved, while field 9 is client text that the signer, the verifier and the server's authorisation must all read identically. An implementation that reuses its key_id normaliser for field 9 passes v28 and fails u06, u07 and u08.

v19 and v20 are a permutation pair: the same two elements in both orders, with different signatures. The server resolves a repeated key to its last occurrence, so the two targets mean different things. A verifier that accepted one signature for both would accept a request whose meaning was not signed.
Body-size-cap vectors (a body exactly at the cap, and one byte over, expecting 413) are not included. The body size limit is a server-side admission control, not a canonicalisation rule.

generated_under.note: The environment that generated this table. The server parser contract below is declared, not measured here.

server_parser_contract.note: The HTTP parser the server's path and query handling is specified against. Declared, not measured by this repository. If the server's parser changes, the vectors must be checked again.

vectors.description: GET with no query and no body. The body field is the SHA-256 of zero bytes, never of '{}' and never empty; the query field is the empty string and its separators remain. The request has no Content-Type, so field 8 is the empty string by the same convention.

POST with a compact JSON body. The bytes hashed are the bytes sent, never a re-serialization. Content-Type is 'application/json' with no parameters; compare v32 and v33, same bytes with parameters, three different signatures.

Query keys arrive in a non-alphabetical order and are signed in that order. A sorting implementation emits 'archived=false&cursor=abc&limit=10' here and produces a different signature, so this vector fails against one.
A key with no '=' keeps that distinction from a key with an empty value: 'flag' stays 'flag'. Submission order is preserved, so this is 'flag&flag=&a=1', not the sorted 'a=1&flag&flag='.
'?a=' is an empty value, distinct from '?a'.
Repeated keys keep their submission order: 'tag=zeta&tag=alpha&tag=beta' signs in exactly that order. The server resolves a repeated key to its last occurrence, so the order carries meaning.
%2F in the path is not decoded: '/a%2Fb' and '/a/b' are different requests with different signatures.
Percent-encoding case is preserved: '%2f' is not normalized to '%2F'. Compare with v07: same route, different signature.
'+' in a query value stays '+'. Nothing is decoded and nothing is re-encoded, so '+' is not read as a space.
'//' in the path is preserved, not collapsed.
A non-ASCII path segment is signed in its percent-encoded UTF-8 form (cafe with an acute accent). No Unicode normalization is applied: NFC and NFD spellings are different bytes and sign differently.
A body containing bytes that are not valid UTF-8 (0xff 0xfe 0x00 0x01) hashes normally: the body is hashed as bytes, never as text.
A trailing '/' is significant: compare with v01, same route, different signature.
DELETE with a query and no body, so the body field is the empty-body digest.
Empty elements between '&' separators are retained in place, so 'a=1&&b=2' canonicalizes to 'a=1&&b=2'. A sorting implementation moves the empty element to the front and emits '&a=1&b=2'.
An '=' inside a value needs no rule at all when the bytes are emitted verbatim: 'filter=a=b&z=1' signs as itself. There is no key/value split in which the distinction could be lost.
A UTF-8 body with non-ASCII text, hashed as the encoded bytes.

vectors.description: An explicitly empty body (zero bytes) is identical to no body at all.

Permutation pair, member A. With v20: the same two elements in both orders. The server resolves a repeated key to its last occurrence, so v19 means org=victim and v20 means org=attacker, and their signatures must differ. A sorting implementation returns 'org=attacker&org=victim' for both and produces one signature for two different requests.
Permutation pair, member B: v19's elements in reverse submission order. Compare the signatures with v19: they must not be equal.

A non-alphabetical query whose sorted form differs from its submission form: 'flag=&flag&a=1' signs as itself, where a sorting implementation emits 'a=1&flag&flag='. This vector cannot pass against one.

Path normalisation step 1 decodes unreserved escapes only: '%7e' becomes '~', so the path field is '/v1/files/a~b'. Compare with v23 and v24: all three have one signature. A signature covers every target that normalises to the same path, because the server acts on the normalised path.

Both hex cases decode: '%7E' becomes '~' exactly as '%7e' does. Same signature as v22 and v24. Contrast v07/v08, where '%2F' and '%2f' are reserved, are not decoded, and therefore keep their hex-case difference and sign differently.
The same path with the character sent literally. A signer that emits raw_path verbatim gives v24 this signature and gives v22 and v23 two others, so it agrees here and fails there.

Path normalisation step 2 removes dot segments (RFC 3986 5.2.4): '/v1/x/../components' signs as '/v1/components'. HTTP clients and the server both remove dot segments, so the normalised path is the one every hop agrees on.
'/./' is removed too: '/v1/./components' signs as '/v1/components'. Same signature as v25 and v27.

Step order. '%2E' is unreserved, so step 1 decodes it to '.' and step 2 then removes it as a dot segment: '/v1/x/%2E%2E/components' signs as '/v1/components'. An implementation that removes dot segments first finds none to remove and emits '/v1/x/../components' instead. This is the only vector that distinguishes the two orders.

Key id normalisation. 'key_id_input' is the same UUID as every other vector's, supplied in uppercase. Field 3 is the lowercase 8-4-4-4-12 form, so this vector's canonical_request and signature are identical to v01's. An implementation that uses the string as supplied produces a different signature here and agrees everywhere else. Normalise by parsing the UUID and rendering it again. Braced, unhyphenated and uppercase forms all normalise to the same field 3.

A POST that carries body bytes and no Content-Type header. Field 8 is the empty string, the same convention the query field uses: not a guessed default and not an omitted field. An implementation that defaults an absent header to 'application/octet-stream' produces a different signature here and agrees everywhere else.

Boundary pair, member A. The body bytes are identical to v31 and only the multipart 'boundary' parameter differs. Signing Content-Type prevents the same signed bytes from being re-framed so that the server's multipart parser reads different parts from them. Because Content-Type is signed verbatim, the two sign differently. An implementation that reduces it to the media type and drops parameters emits one signature for both.

vectors.description: A well-formed Perceivo-Organization on a request that also carries a body and a Content-Type, so field 9 is exercised in a realistic shape rather than only in isolation. Field 9 is the header verbatim, lowercase hyphenated 8-4-4-4-12. Compare with v02, the same request with no organization header: the signatures differ.

Organization pair, member A. Identical to v36 in method, target, body and Content-Type; only the organization differs. Only v34, v35 and v36 sign a non-empty organization, so these are the rows that fail if an implementation omits field 9. It is also the same request as v01, which sends no header: three requests, three signatures.

Organization pair, member B: same request, different organization. Compare the signatures with v35: they must not be equal. An implementation that omits field 9, or signs a constant there, emits one signature for both, so a signature captured for one organization would verify when presented with the other's header.

negative_vectors.description: Six fields: METHOD, path, query, body digest, timestamp and nonce of v01's request, correctly signed. A verifier that accepts it leaves the domain, audience, key id, Content-Type and organization fields unchecked. Reject on the field count before comparing digests: eleven fields, ten separators, no trailing newline.
Nine fields: v01's canonical request without the Content-Type and organization fields, correctly signed. Reject on the field count.

Field 1 is 'perceivo-hmac-v2'. The field count is correct, so only the domain comparison rejects this request. The domain is a constant and is compared for exact equality, so a signature produced for another scheme with the same secret cannot be replayed here.

Field 2 is 'perceivo-api-prod' where this verifier is configured for 'perceivo-api-local'. The field count is correct. Correctly signed and rejected: a request signed for one deployment must not verify at another. The verifier compares field 2 with its own configured audience, never with the request's Host header.

Field 3 is '3d1c1a7e-6b54-4b0e-9a2d-8c5f0e21b4aa' while the bearer header names '0f8fad5b-d9cb-469f-a165-70867728950e', whose secret was used. The field count is correct. Correctly signed and rejected: the verifier compares field 3 with the id of the key whose secret it used, so a signature cannot be presented under a different key.

Ten fields: v01's canonical request with the organization field omitted rather than empty, correctly signed. Accepting it leaves field 9 unbound, so a captured signature could be presented with another organization. It differs from v01, which signs field 9 as the empty string: the value is the same, the field count is not, and only the field count check distinguishes them.

Field 9 binding. Eleven fields; fields 1, 2 and 3 are correct; the MAC is correct. Field 9 names '1a4f6d20-9e3b-47c8-85af-b62d0c17e995' while the request carried '8c7e2b41-5d93-4a06-bf12-3e9d70a5c684' (see presented_organization). A verifier must read field 9 from the signed string after compare_digest and reject a value that differs from the header it received (signature_metadata_unbound), as it does for the timestamp and nonce. The comparison must follow the MAC check: before it, both values are unauthenticated client input. An implementation that signs field 9 but never compares it passes every other row and fails only this one.

unsignable_vectors.description: A Content-Type whose parameter contains U+00E9, sent as UTF-8 bytes. Field 8 admits printable ASCII, 0x20-0x7E, only, so the signer must refuse it. A latin-1 decoder and a UTF-8 decoder read these bytes as different text ('Ã©' and 'é') and would sign different values; on printable ASCII the two agree.

A single 0xFF byte, which is not valid UTF-8. A UTF-8 decoder refuses it before the character check; a latin-1 decoder reaches the character check and refuses it there. The vector specifies the outcome, not which check produces it.

A newline in Content-Type. 0x0A is outside 0x20-0x7E, so the character rule also covers the rule that no field may contain a newline. Rejected, never escaped: escaping would produce a string no other implementation would reproduce.
A horizontal tab (0x09) between parameters. RFC 7230 admits it as optional whitespace inside a header value; this format does not.
0x7F (DEL), one past the top of the admitted range. The boundary is closed at 0x7E, so this pins the upper edge; 0x7E itself ('~') is signable and appears in the positive controls.

The same UUID as v35's, in uppercase. Field 9 is rejected rather than converted to lowercase, unlike the key id in v28, which normalises to the canonical spelling and produces v01's signature. The key id is a UUID the server has already resolved; field 9 is client text that the signer, the verifier and the server's authorisation must all read identically.
The UUID in braces. Refused for u06's reason: field 9 has one admissible spelling.
The 32-character unhyphenated form. Refused for u06's reason. `uuid.UUID()` accepts this spelling, so an implementation that validates by parsing rather than by matching the pattern accepts it.
An organization slug rather than a UUID. Field 9 is a UUID or the empty string; a signer must refuse anything else rather than sign a request the server will reject.

A newline inside the organization value. Rejected, never escaped: a newline in a field adds a field, which the verifier's field count check rejects. Escaping would produce a string no other implementation would reproduce.

Two Perceivo-Organization headers. Rejected rather than resolved: if the signer picked one value, the server's verifier and its authorisation could pick differently. Read the header as a list of values; a mapping built from the headers collapses duplicates and hides this case.

secret_transport_vectors.description: The issued form. The 64-character hex secret decoded to its 32 bytes, which are the bytes the server keys on. This is the row every implementation must reproduce.

The incorrect encoding, published so it can be recognised. The same secret encoded as UTF-8 instead of decoded from hex: a 64-byte key where the server holds a 32-byte one. Must not verify. If your signature for t01 equals this value, the secret is being encoded rather than decoded; the canonical request, timestamp and nonce are not the cause.
The same 32 bytes written in uppercase hex. Hex decoding is case-insensitive, so this signature is identical to t01's. An implementation that rejects the uppercase spelling fails here.
A secret that is not 64 hex characters. `secret_utf8` is keyed on its UTF-8 bytes, so this signature is identical to v01's.

64 characters, one of them outside the hex alphabet. Keyed on its UTF-8 bytes, because an issued secret is recognised by its alphabet and its length together. An implementation that decodes on length alone fails here. A 64-character passphrase made only of hex characters cannot be told apart from an issued secret and is decoded; to key on such text, pass bytes.
